title: 不簡單，“吃貨快樂榜”也全面AI化了
abstract: 不簡單，“吃貨快樂榜”也全面AI化了 林, 方舟 2026-09-11 16:59:28 來源： 量子位 林方舟 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 家人們，高德掃街榜推出一年了，有沒有人和我一樣，現在乾飯前總要刷一刷它？ 去年，依靠真實導航和到店行為資料，高德直接在美食和到店領域來了一波諾曼底登陸。 但我以為這也就到頭了。 沒想到，時隔一年，高德9月10日宣佈： 掃街榜全面AI化了 。 大模型化，世界模型助力，開啟空間智慧覓食新時代。 How？ 升級後的2026版掃街榜，用AI算法理解不同導航到店行為的評分權重，更精準體現使用者真實選擇，讓更多經得起反覆考驗的寶藏好店脫穎而出。 而高德如此升級背後的技術，正是最前沿的 空間智慧 。 要知道，空間智慧可是現在世界模型圈子裡的頂流，李飛飛團隊的Atlas剛發出來時，朋友圈都快被刷爆了。 而高德，早就不是你以為的那個“只會導航的地圖App”了。人家攢了二十多年時空資料，業務遍佈物理世界的犄角旮旯，搞空間智慧屬於是“專業對口”。 特別是高德空間智慧的核心引擎——ABot-Earth 0.7，被稱為 “全球首個3D原生城市世界模型” 。 這玩意兒有多猛？僅需一張衛星圖或一段文字，在消費級GPU上跑10分鐘，它就能給你生成一座擁有真實街景的3D城市，效率比傳統方法提升了1000倍。 一個字：夯！ “3D原生”路線，效率和價效比拉滿 人在中關村工位，突然想像梁朝偉一樣任性一把，飛去倫敦喂鴿子…… 於是我開啟訂票軟體，哦不對，開啟“高德地球”的官網，餵給它一張倫敦特拉法加廣場的衛星圖。 沒過多久，它就給我生成了一個1平方公里的“真實世界”，建築錯落有致，植被層次分明，地標還原逼真…… 雲逛了一會後，摸魚結束，意滿離～ 讓我穿越到英倫的“魔法”，正是ABot-Earth 0.7。 無論是浪漫的土耳其，還是東京和巴黎，ABot-Earth 0.7都能帶我抵達。按照團隊的說法，目前它已囊括190多個國家、300多座城市，建成了 全球覆蓋國家和地區數量最多的3D地圖 。 反觀大家熟悉的Google Earth，只有少數大都市的核心區才有3D場景的待遇，廣大中小城市和欠發達地區還停留在二維的衛星圖片時代。 把一座城市搬進三維世界，是個費時費錢的大工程。以Google Earth採用的傳統三維重建為例，先要採集影像，再計算建築的位置和形狀，最後還得還原表面的紋理。要覆蓋更多地方、更新更多場景，這些工作就得持續投入。一套流程下來，更新一次動輒數月甚至數年，家裡有礦才敢這麼玩。 ABot-Earth 0.7想降低的，正是生成下一個三維場景的成本。 它先用大量真實的室外場景三維重建資料訓練模型，讓模型學會城市和地貌的空間規律：道路怎麼延伸，街區如何排布，建築、植被與水體怎樣分佈。這些看似複雜的地表資訊，其實都有跡可循。 有了這樣的基礎，模型拿到一張衛星圖或少量地面資訊，就能根據已有線索推斷空間結構、補全細節，快速生成結構合理、外觀逼真的三維場景。過去積累的三維資料，由此支撐起更多新場景的生成，也讓高保真三維內容能夠以更低成本、更大規模生產出來。 這裡插播一個知識點：三維高斯（3DGS）。你可以把它想像成空間裡一團團帶顏色、有透明度的“小橢球棉花糖”。無數個這樣的棉花糖堆在一起，就變成了樓房、樹木和馬路。 ABot-Earth 0.7說的“3D原生”，就是模型直接學習並生成這些“棉花糖”，輸出結果天生自帶3D結構，想從哪個角度看都行。 但問題來了：一塊城區就有數百萬個“棉花糖”，就算你有再多卡，它也吃不消啊！ 於是高德設計了原生3DGS壓縮與重建方案：“先壓縮，再生成”。訓練時把複雜的3D場景壓成緊湊的“潛空間壓縮包”；生成時在潛空間裡搞定，再解壓成三維高斯。 這套方案兼顧高壓縮率與高質量重建，既降低訓練和推理的開銷，也提升場景的幾何質量 ，讓建築立面更規整、地面更平整，為高效生成高保真三維場景打下基礎。 這就好比你不直接搬運整座圖書館，而是先做成電子書，下載後再列印，省時省力還省硬碟。 更重要的是，原生3D很吃資料的質量。為此，高德先用自研引擎ABot-3DGS，把衛星、航空、街景等多源影像重建成城市級3D場景，再通過高效的3D與2D資料清洗流水線，篩選出高質量、高精度的訓練資料，讓模型從真實世界中學習豐富的空間結構與外觀細節。 正是嚴選高質量的真實3D資料，才保證了生成內容既好看又靠譜，不會出現“路飛到天上、樓長在水裡”的靈異事件。 未來的數字地球，不僅能看還能“盤” 聊完輸入，再聊聊輸出體驗。 ABot-Earth 0.7給我的感覺就倆字：絲滑。 滑鼠滾輪狂滾，從蔚藍地球秒切城市全景，再無縫鑽到具體街道，中間幾乎沒有卡頓，比我彙報工作還流暢。 這種絲滑體驗得益於高德設計的原生3DGS多層次解碼器（LOD），它可以在不進行昂貴後處理的情況下，直接生成層次化的三維高斯結構，主打一個“即時線上，拒絕載入條”。 當我瀏覽大面積的地圖時，也幾乎沒有發現拼接錯位，也沒有遇到載入卡頓。 ABot-Earth 0.7採用了一種高效的滑窗推理機制，在重疊區域進行智慧融合，極大地消除了拼接痕跡，能生成近乎無縫的地球級場景。這套方案讓場景的破洞率、破損率降低了97%，區域邊界過渡自然平滑，單次推理即可完成超過10平方公里的三維場景生成。 不過，ABot-Earth 0.7也有自己的能力邊界。 比如衛星影像看不到建築立面，需要模型自己“腦補”。所以雖然它生成的畫面逼真，但並不意味著每扇窗戶都與現實一一對應。 因此，對於埃菲爾鐵塔、羅馬鬥獸場這種知名地標，高德採取了“大片城區由ABot-Earth 0.7生成、地標使用3D生成模型製作，再通過Agent自動校準拼接”的方式，獲得了“混搭”的視覺效果。 高德通過世界模型能力，從有限實景照片等多模態輸入生成高質量可漫遊的3DGS場景，把生成能力從“上帝視角”推進到“街景級細節”，通過自增強空間生成技術突破了傳統級聯生成中誤差隨輪次累積、紋理與幾何逐輪退化的問題，使模型的生成範圍顯著擴大、紋理質量顯著提升，實現從城市級到街道級的真實感3D遊覽。 這也意味著，數字地球將不再只是被動觀看的“電子沙盤”，而會成為可生成、可模擬、可編輯的動態空間智慧平臺。 高德CEO郭寧將模型對真實世界的理解拆解為四個層次： 二維網路拓撲：描述道路、建築與地點如何連線； 三維空間：呈現世界的物理結構； 時間的變化：讓同一空間在不同時刻呈現不同狀態； 真實世界的流動：人流、車流等行為路徑。 四層資訊疊加在一起，構成高德所定義的 空間智慧 。 用這個框架來看ABot-Earth 0.7，它目前解決了“三維空間”的高效構建問題，同時保留了與“二維網路拓撲”的精確對齊，為後續疊加“時間的變化”和“真實世界的流動”打下了地基。 在這個意義上，ABot-Earth 0.7不只是技術產品，更是AI “理解真實世界的入口” 。 Benchmark只是基本功，使用者買賬才是真本事 ABot-Earth 0.7很強，但它也只是高德空間智慧中的一環。 按照李飛飛給世界模型的分類框架（渲染器、模擬器、規劃器），高德是業內少有的在同一個架構裡把三者都做了一遍的公司。 渲染器負責3D呈現，對應高德的ABot-World、ABot-Earth系列、ABot-Recon和雲境、飛行街景2.0等產品； 模擬器負責對現實世界進行預測與模擬，在高德語境下體現為未來交通態勢推演、商圈客流預測等能力； 規劃器則在理解與預測之後，為各類Agent輸出具體行動指令，比如高德ABot全棧具身技術體系中的ABot-Navigation（導航模型）和ABot-Manipulation（操作模型），可直接部署在機器人上指導移動與操作；以及能夠超視距預警的高德鷹眼守護。 這三者共享底層的因果Transformer架構。不同模態的輸入（影像、文本、點雲、交通流等）經過各自編碼器處理後，進入共享注意力機制。既保持獨立表徵，又實現跨模態互通。 這種設計讓高德能在一個統一框架內，同時支撐C端體驗最佳化、B端數字孿生服務和具身智慧落地，而不是為每個場景單獨訓練一套模型。 打個比方，這套架構像一場多語種聯合國大會：不同模態資訊先由各自的“同聲傳譯”（編碼器）轉成通用語言，再圍坐在同一張圓桌（共享注意力機制）旁對話協作，既聽得懂彼此，又不丟失各自的表達方式。 目前，包括ABot體系在內的高德空間智慧前沿模型及研究在全球獲得20多項冠軍和SOTA。 但高德說了： Benchmark刷分只是基本功，真實使用者買賬才是真本事。 畢竟堵車的時候，司機才不管你後臺用了什麼神仙模型，只想知道這條路還能不能走。 除基礎導航外，自2025年提出全面AI化以來，高德已經把空間智慧用到了多種場景，比如推出開放環境全自主具身機器人高德途途、釋出專為具身智慧打造的城市級模擬訓練場，並推出紅綠燈倒計時和高德鷹眼守護以及全面AI化的掃街榜2026等產品。 在高德看來，數字世界中的智慧，最終都要在物理世界裡找到自身的價值。 未來，空間智慧將如雲計算一樣，成為各行各業與物理世界互動的標配基礎能力。 以前，高德是連線人和現實世界的基礎設施；現在，高德正在變成連線機器人和物理世界的基礎設施。 當你在掃街榜上精準找到一家寶藏小館，當無人機在摩天大樓叢中自主避障，當智慧汽車在晚高峰預判擁堵、提前變道——這些看似不相關的場景，底層是同一套 空間智慧體系 。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 世界模型 title: 墨芯人工智慧亮相2026 Inclusion·外灘大會：以專用稀疏推理晶片提升算力效能，共創AI新經濟
abstract: 墨芯人工智慧亮相2026 Inclusion·外灘大會：以專用稀疏推理晶片提升算力效能，共創AI新經濟 量子位的朋友們 2026-09-11 14:19:03 來源： 量子位 9月9日，墨芯人工智慧亮相以”共創AI新經濟”為主題的2026 Inclusion·外灘大會。 9月9日，作為螞蟻集團生態合作夥伴，墨芯人工智慧亮相以”共創AI新經濟”為主題的2026 Inclusion·外灘大會。大會期間，墨芯展示了AI計算卡產品，全面呈現了以專用稀疏推理晶片提升算力效能、助力AI新經濟發展的技術路徑。 推理需求攀升，算力效能成為發展AI新經濟關鍵變數 當前，人工智慧技術成果正加速轉化為面向數字空間和物理世界的產品與服務，推動AI新經濟加快形成，算力需求隨之持續增長，尤其是推理側需求大幅攀升。提升算力效能，可以在同等計算資源下完成更多推理任務，為AI產品和服務的規模化發展提供重要支撐，進一步釋放AI新經濟的發展潛力。 墨芯以專用稀疏推理晶片提升算力效能，助力拓展AI新經濟應用空間 面對持續增長的推理需求，在增加算力供給的同時，還需通過計算方式創新提升算力效能。作為稀疏計算引領者，墨芯人工智慧通過演算法、軟體與硬體三位一體協同最佳化，以專用稀疏推理晶片減少冗餘計算、提升計算效率，讓有限算力完成更多有效計算，為AI新經濟發展提供更高效的計算方式。 目前，墨芯基於自研晶片構建的推理叢集已在西北、西南、華東、華北四大片區的資料中心實現部署，並結合各地產業與資源特點，為智慧製造、生命科學、城市治理等不同場景提供高效推理支撐，推動算力與產業需求加快結合，共同拓展AI新經濟的應用空間。 隨著AI應用不斷深入，推理負載也呈現出更加多樣和動態的特徵，對晶片的資料處理與排程能力提出了新的要求。為此，墨芯即將推出新一代SparsePrime®計算卡，通過架構升級和排程機制最佳化，進一步滿足不斷演進的AI推理需求。 從技術創新到生態建設，共創AI新經濟 要讓更高效的計算方式真正服務於AI新經濟，不僅需要持續推進技術與產品創新，還需要降低技術適配與產業協同的門檻。墨芯在推進專用稀疏推理晶片規模化落地的同時，也進一步參與行業標準研製，推動產學研合作，與各方共建繁榮的AI算力生態。 今年7月，墨芯成為工業和資訊化部人工智慧標準化技術委員會成員單位，將依託稀疏計算領域的技術積累與產業化實踐，參與AI基礎硬體、軟體平臺及大模型等方向的標準研製，推動晶片、軟體、模型與應用之間更高效協同，降低產業鏈上下游的適配成本和AI技術規模化應用門檻。 8月，墨芯發起成立稀疏計算產學研聯盟，圍繞前沿研究、關鍵技術攻關和成果轉化開展協同創新，推動科研創新轉化為AI新經濟的發展動能。 AI產品與服務加速規模化應用，正持續釋放AI新經濟的發展潛力。墨芯將持續推進計算方式創新，以專用稀疏推理晶片提升算力效能，讓有限算力承載更多智慧應用，推動AI生產力在千行百業加快落地。 本文由墨芯人工智慧提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 墨芯人工智慧 量子位的朋友們 量子位「MEET2027智慧未來大會」啟動！年度榜單徵集進行中 2026-09-11 全球瘋狂「搶單」，中國智駕黑馬浮現：蔣京芳為何選擇neueHCT？ 2026-09-10 全球首個3D原生城市世界模型ABot-Earth 0.7釋出，構建AI理解真實世界的入口 2026-09-10 全球首個可模擬的人–場景互動重建框架 HSImul3R：讓人類影片真正成為機器人技能來源 2026-09-10 相關閱讀

title: 量子位「MEET2027智慧未來大會」啟動！年度榜單徵集進行中
abstract: 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI AI，正變得前所未有的“能幹”。 以前我們用AI，大多隻是開啟對話方塊提問；如今變化早已發生在對話方塊之外—— 智慧體能自主拆解目標、排程工具、跑完整條任務流程，中途出錯還能折回修正； 機器人從實驗室演示影片走進 產線、倉庫和門店 ，開始承擔真實作業； 世界模型教會機器 理解物理規律 ，而不僅僅把語料擬合得更像人話。 也正因如此，衡量AI好不好用，也就不能比誰在榜單上多拿幾分，現在要看它能不能在真實環境裡把活幹完、幹穩、幹得敢交付。 而AI一旦開始替人做決定、動手執行，可靠性、可控性、安全邊界這些關鍵詞，就成了產業和社會都繞不開的問題。 我們與其說是在等一個未來到來，不如說是在學著怎麼駕馭它。 於是，在如此背景之下，我們將以 「智行合一，馭見未來」 為主題，正式啟動 MEET2027智慧未來大會！ 承襲MEET系列年度行業觀察的視角，誠邀科技、產業與學術領域的領軍人物齊聚一堂，共同見證行業變革。 「智行合一」 ，說的是智慧與行動終於合到了一處——理解、規劃、執行、反饋，過去分散在多套系統裡的環節，如今被壓進同一個閉環。智慧體從聊天走向作業，具身智慧給模型配上身體，世界模型將虛實打通，AI更已深入 科研、製造、能源、交通 等產業腹地，乾的遠不止降本增效。 「馭見未來」 ，是因為未來不會自己走過來給人看，它得有人駕馭。當智慧開始承擔決策與執行，可靠、可控、可解釋就從技術議題變成了公共議題。誰能駕馭它，誰才有資格談下一個十年。 知行合一，方能行穩致遠 ——走到深水區的“人工智慧+”，最值得認真討論的大概就是這件事。 MEET2027智慧未來大會 今年是 MEET智慧未來大會 的第八年。過去七屆，上百位產業與學術嘉賓登上過MEET舞臺—— 李開復博士、張亞勤博士 等產業代表， 倪光南院士、譚建榮院士、李培根院士、鄭緯民院士，以及周志華教授、唐傑教授等學術界代表；百度、阿里、騰訊、華為、京東、美團、小米、商湯 等科技領軍企業均曾深度參與。 正是這些獨到的行業觀點，讓參會人數屢創新高。每年大會都能吸引 上千名科技從業者 到場， 數百萬觀眾線上圍觀，近百家合作媒體 聯合曝光，MEET智慧未來大會也因此成了智慧科技行業的年度風向標。 點選檢視MEET2026回顧： 「連結」 今年，我們把鏡頭對準AI從“能想”走向“能幹”的關鍵一躍，誠邀 技術、產業、投資領域 有代表性的企業和人物，共同探討智慧體、具身智慧與機器人、AI Infra與算力、世界模型、智慧終端、智慧駕駛、低空經濟、AI for Science、能源電力等年度議題。 12月，等你來和我們共論智慧落地的破局之道。 重磅釋出：2026人工智慧年度榜單 量子位 「人工智慧年度榜單」 已成為AI行業最具影響力的榜單之一。今年是智慧技術從演示走向交付的一年，跑得快的很多，走得實的不多。我們希望通過年度評選，把那些真正把智慧變成生產力、把想法做成產品的公司和人物找出來，向他們致敬。 榜單從企業、產品、人物三大維度展開，共評選五類獎項，結果將在MEET2027大會上正式釋出。 報名截止：2026年11月16日 評選結果將於量子位主辦的MEET2027智慧未來大會上正式公佈。 網頁端連結：https://wj.qq.com/s2/27813867/cbwi/ 年度AI十大趨勢報告同步釋出 按照每年慣例，年度趨勢系列報告也會在MEET2027大會上重磅釋出。 點選檢視《2025年度AI十大趨勢報告》： 「連結」 量子位智庫今年繼續錨定AI這一時代科技發展的主旋律，站在新進展與新資訊的最前沿、產學研交匯的核心地帶，與各位共赴下一場智慧浪潮。 結合技術成熟度、落地現狀、潛在價值等因素，《2026年度AI十大趨勢報告》將提名正在釋放巨大潛力的十大AI趨勢，並對各趨勢做深入分析，提名代表機構與最佳案例，敬請期待。 會議設定 時間：2026年12月 地點：中國·北京 參會方式：報名通道即將開啟，請關注量子位公眾號後續資訊。 聯絡方式 商務合作 陳飛 郵箱：chenfei@qbitai.com 活動合作 劉天宇 微信：13681181332 郵箱：liutianyu@qbitai.com

title: 3萬臺無人車之後，這家公司盯上了城市級物理AI
abstract: 3萬臺無人車之後，這家公司盯上了城市級物理AI 思邈 2026-09-11 10:50:47 來源： 量子位 允中 發自 副駕寺 智慧車參考 | 公眾號 AI4Auto 如果把過去幾年自動駕駛產業的發展放在一起看，會發現一個明顯的變化：行業討論的重點，正在從“自動駕駛能不能跑”，轉向“自動駕駛如何真正進入現實世界”。 尤其在物流配送領域，無人車正在從早期的技術驗證和限定場景測試，進入規模化商業運營階段。 車輛數量增加、運營城市擴大之後，單純討論一輛車的自動駕駛能力已經不夠，如何讓無人車進入更多行業、形成穩定運力，並進一步融入城市物流和產業體系，正在成為新的問題。 這也是九識此次戰略升級的背景。 9月10日，九識在廣州舉行戰略釋出會。會上，九識宣佈完成“ 城市級物理AI ”的戰略升級，通過“九識大腦”賦能更多城市治理場景。 釋出會現場，九識面向快遞物流、商貿配送、城市短駁等多場景推出“ 九識租車 ”小程式。同時，九識還開放了“ 九識租車 ”的無人運力加盟，並公佈針對首批加盟合作夥伴的專屬優惠政策。 與此同時，九識還與廣汽領程、廣州公交集團、廣環投、廣州歐緯德、尚元、九識極景等產業夥伴簽署合作協議，合作範圍涉及無人車製造、城市服務、產學研等領域。 新增圖片註釋，不超過 140 字（可選） 從發明RoboVan、實現無人車真正的規模化運營，到九識租車、Zelos Inside合作，這些看似分散的動作背後，其實對應著九識過去五年的一條發展路徑： 先把無人車真正做出來，再讓無人車進入更多真實場景，最終把已經驗證的技術和運營能力變成可以連線城市與產業的基礎能力。 從RoboVan開始，九識奠定物理AI的現實入口 五年前，RoboVan還是一個並不常見的概念。 與主要面向乘用車的Robotaxi不同，RoboVan瞄準的是城市物流中大量存在的廂式貨車需求。它需要面對城市公開道路中更加複雜的真實環境，同時還要滿足物流運輸對於裝載、續航、可靠性和運營效率的要求。 九識從城市物流切入，也由此成為RoboVan這一產品形態的開創者。 2023年，九識推出全球首臺RoboVan，並推動其進入城市公開道路運營。此後，九識持續圍繞車輛產品、自動駕駛系統和規模化運營進行迭代，將一輛能夠自動駕駛的車，逐漸變成能夠真正承擔物流任務的生產工具。 這也是九識過去五年最重要的一層積累：把自動駕駛技術做深做透，讓無人車能跑、能用、好用，更能夠在真實道路上長期穩定執行。 而要從“能跑”走向規模化運營，安全是繞不開的一道門檻。 新增圖片註釋，不超過 140 字（可選） 九識CEO孔旗表示： “安全不是規模化之後才去解決的問題。而是從第一天開始，就必須建立起來的能力。” 在自動駕駛技術層面，九識通過持續的資料閉環，將實際道路運營中積累的經驗反饋至演算法和系統迭代，不斷提升無人車對複雜道路環境的理解與應對能力。 在功能安全和效能安全方面，九識圍繞車輛控制、通訊等關鍵環節進行安全冗餘設計，並針對車輛的穩定性、可靠性等開展數千項測試。今年，九識成立了行業首個安全委員會，從組織機制和技術體系兩個層面持續推進無人車安全管理與能力建設。 這些看起來並不“性感”的基礎能力，卻決定了無人車能不能從幾輛測試車，變成一支真正可以長期運營的車隊。 隨著產品不斷規模化，九識的無人車開始進入快遞快運、商超零售、輪胎汽配、醫藥等不同場景。如今，九識已經在全球 300多座城市 實現常態化運營，累計運營里程突破 2.5億公里 。 對於L4自動駕駛來說，真實道路上的每一公里，都是對無人車自動駕駛系統以及運營體系的一次驗證。規模化運營讓九識不斷面對不同城市、不同道路和不同物流任務，也讓自動駕駛能力從實驗環境走向更加複雜的現實世界。 過去幾年，九識也逐漸形成成熟的無人駕駛商業範式。通過整車售賣、金融分期服務、自動駕駛訂閱服務等模式，不斷降低客戶的用車門檻。這也促成了九識組建出全球最大的RoboVan車隊，根據九識最新的公開資料，其車隊規模目前 超過3萬臺 ，服務於中國郵政、順豐、三通一達、蒙牛、新希望、中策橡膠等全球知名企業和大量中小型客戶，市場佔比穩居第一。 可即便無人車行業的發展已經遠超預期，但九識仍發現了物流行業中仍有大量的需求，無法通過落地無人車直接滿足。 從無人車到無人運力，九識開啟城市應用空間 租車的運營模式，來自無人車真實的運營場景。 2025年初，九識崑山的使用者阿綱購買了4臺九識無人車，最初嘗試將車輛出租給有配送需求的客戶。隨著需求增加，他的車輛規模從4臺擴大到幾十臺，如今已增加到200多臺。 車越來越多之後，阿綱開始做另一件事：通過拼單、拼時等方式重新組織車輛的閒置時間，讓同一批無人車能夠在不同時間服務不同客戶，提高整體使用效率。 從4臺車到200多臺車，這個案例讓九識看到，在無人車逐漸普及之後，城市物流對無人駕駛的需求可能正在發生變化。 過去，客戶獲取無人車的主要方式是採購。一旦購買車輛，就意味著一次性的資產投入，同時還要承擔車輛管理、運營維護以及閒置帶來的成本。 但對於很多運輸需求具有波動性的企業而言，他們真正需要的可能並不是一輛無人車，而是一項穩定的運輸能力。 “客戶真正關心的，可能不是我要買一輛什麼車，而是我每天有沒有 穩定的運輸能力 ，這輛車能不能 按照我的需求工作 。”九識CEO孔旗在釋出會上表示。 新增圖片註釋，不超過 140 字（可選） 洞察到這一需求後，九識迅速行動，在全國45座城市、300家客戶的真實場景中進行租賃模式試點，累計完成1500+筆租賃訂單，累計執行里程超過100萬公里。 此次釋出會上，九識正式推出“九識租車”。日租、月租、年租等靈活的無人車使用方式，讓企業可以根據實際業務需求獲取無人運輸能力。同時，九識也開放城市無人運力加盟，希望通過更多本地合作夥伴，將車輛、客戶和運輸需求進一步組織起來。 九識提供無人車以及車輛管理、智慧排程等平臺能力，本地合作夥伴則可以利用自身在物流、商貿、運輸等領域的資源，將無人車投入快遞、商超、商貿配送等城市物流場景。 如果說過去五年九識解決的是“無人車如何真正跑起來”，那麼九識租車正在嘗試解決的，就是“跑起來之後，如何讓這批車被更加高效地使用”。其商業模式也開始從“銷售裝置”，向“提供運力”延伸。 而這也是無人駕駛從技術產品走向城市基礎運力的重要一步。 產業協同，九識讓物理AI走向更大規模 過去，一家公司可以通過自己研發、自己造車、自己運營，完成一個無人駕駛專案。但當車輛進入更多城市、更多產業和更多車型之後，僅靠一家公司獨立完成所有環節，顯然很難支撐更大的規模。 過去五年，九識積累的不只是車輛規模，更包括大量來自現實世界的 道路資料、場景經驗和運營能力 。這些能力正在進一步沉澱到“九識大腦”中。 在九識的定義裡，“九識大腦”並不是一套單純的智駕軟體，而是 面向真實世界的AI能力中樞 。它將車輛執行過程中積累的場景和L4運營經驗進一步沉澱、複用，併成為九識從“一輛無人車”走向“城市級物理AI”的核心。 更重要的是，九識正在將這些能力進一步標準化。 一方面，通過標準化產品，把經過真實運營驗證的L4能力快速複製到不同車輛和場景；另一方面，通過Zelos Inside，將自動駕駛系統、AI演算法、軟硬體能力以及規模化運營經驗，輸出給更多車企和產業夥伴。 新增圖片註釋，不超過 140 字（可選） 在此基礎上，九識則一步構建三類城市能力：通過運力管理平臺，讓智慧運力可以被組織和排程；通過運營監測平臺，讓無人車執行狀態可感知、可保障；通過政府監管平臺，讓城市中的無人運營更加可視、可管、可追溯。 九識CEO孔旗介紹， “九識大腦”是九識通過真實世界場景和L4運營經驗沉澱出來的強大智慧核心和面向真實世界的AI能力中樞。 基於九識大腦，九識研發了Robovan產品，並基於Zelos Inside模式，以L4智駕技術與生態夥伴共同開發多品類無人車產品，賦能千行百業。 在此基礎上，九識進一步構建了面向使用者、車輛管理、運營監管的城市級服務平臺，讓無人車從一輛輛獨立執行的智慧車輛，逐漸成為能夠高效服務城市的無人運力。 這使“九識大腦”不只是連線一輛無人車的智慧核心，而成為向下連線車輛和生態產品，向上連線運力、運營和城市治理的一套AI能力體系。 Zelos Inside則承擔了產業協同的另一層角色。 新增圖片註釋，不超過 140 字（可選） 九識此前已經與東風股份等車企展開合作，通過Zelos Inside將L4自動駕駛能力與車企的整車開發和製造能力結合起來，共同推動無人駕駛商用車的開發、驗證和量產落地。 此次釋出會上，九識又與廣汽領程、廣州公交集團、廣環投、尚元、極景等產業夥伴簽署合作協議，合作進一步向更多車型、城市和應用場景延伸。 從打造RoboVan，到運營無人車，再到通過九識租車組織城市無人運力，以及通過Zelos Inside與更多產業夥伴共同拓展場景，九識正在完成一次從“產品公司”向“基礎設施平臺”的演變。 這也是此次九識宣佈完成“城市級物理AI”的戰略升級的核心邏輯。 物理AI最終需要解決的，並不是僅僅完成一次無人駕駛，而是讓AI真正進入現實世界，持續連線車輛、運力、產業與城市，並在真實環境中形成可以被規模化複製的能力。 從一輛RoboVan，到一套城市無人運力，再到連線更多產業的AI能力，九識過去五年的積累，正在進入下一個階段。 — 完 — *本文系智慧車參考獲授權刊載，觀點僅為原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 九識智慧 title: OpenAI這是拿千禧年難題當Benchmark刷啊。。。
abstract: OpenAI這是拿千禧年難題當Benchmark刷啊。。。 一水 2026-09-11 09:46:55 來源： 量子位 爆料直指霍奇猜想 OpenAI的納維-斯托克斯方程連續劇，居然還沒完。。。 《紐約時報》最新追訪，補出了這場衝突中此前沒有披露的細節。 其中最關鍵的一條，是OpenAI更新了關於使用者資料的說法： Buckmaster過去兩個月的Codex提示詞，絕不可能以任何方式影響內部模型。7月3日之後的任何使用者輸入，也不可能進入這套系統 。 這比OpenAI此前 “無法完全排除匿名使用者資料曾幫助改進模型” 的表態明確得多，也給8月研究成果是否進入模型劃出了一條時間線。 不過這仍然是OpenAI單方面給出的說法，目前沒有公開技術材料可供外界獨立核查。 資料爭議還沒落地，OpenAI又扔下一枚炸彈： 攻克納維-斯托克斯之後，公司又在另一道千禧年大獎難題上取得“實質性進展”，正在準備公佈結果 。 而最新傳聞指向的，正是霍奇猜想。 好傢伙，第一道題的論文還在接受審查，第二道題已經要交卷了。 “你為什麼要毀掉自己的職業生涯？” 簡單回顧一下這場爭議始末以及最新爆料。 紐約大學數學家Tristan Buckmaster稱，在自己拒絕OpenAI提出的合作方案，並表示可能公開雙方的溝通經過後，OpenAI研究負責人Sébastien Bubeck對他說： 你為什麼要毀掉自己的職業生涯？ Buckmaster反問，公開事實怎麼會毀掉一名學者的職業生涯。對方又稱： 如果你不希望我保持友善，那我也不必友善。 Bubeck後來承認第一句話確實出自自己之口，但否認是在威脅 。 他隨後曬出自己與Buckmaster合作者Levent Alpöge的聊天截圖。 截圖顯示，Bubeck在電話前提出協調雙方釋出、承認兩人的研究優先權，並願意分享證明和人類提示詞。 但這些訊息只能證明OpenAI在電話前釋放過合作意願，無法還原真正引爆衝突的通話。 《紐約時報》此次補出的，是那場談判更完整的條件 。 當時OpenAI已經完成納維-斯托克斯證明，而Buckmaster和Alpöge只推進到了更簡單的尤拉方程。 OpenAI向Buckmaster提供了幾種選擇： 兩位數學家先發布尤拉方程成果，OpenAI第二天再公佈納維-斯托克斯證明； 由Buckmaster擔任主要作者，重新整理OpenAI模型生成的論文； 為Buckmaster提供充足算力，讓他繼續完成自己的研究； OpenAI還會建議，100萬美元的千禧年大獎榮譽應歸Buckmaster和合作者。 需要說明的是，OpenAI不是要直接支付100萬美元，也沒有證據顯示雙方討論過封口協議。 這裡指的是OpenAI願意公開推薦獎金歸屬。 但Buckmaster仍然覺得，OpenAI是在“收買”自己。 癥結就在他的合作者Alpöge身上 。 Alpöge雖然任職於Anthropic，但這項研究是他的個人業餘專案，並非Anthropic發起。 可Bubeck在接受《紐約時報》採訪時直接確認，OpenAI確實不希望Alpöge出現在最終論文中： 在我們看來，怎麼能讓一名Anthropic員工參與OpenAI內部專案？ Buckmaster則認為，兩人的研究既使用了Anthropic的Claude，也使用了OpenAI的Codex，最合理的辦法應該是兩家公司放下競爭，共同處理這項成果。 他形容，OpenAI無法理解自己為什麼不接受這筆交易，也無法理解他為什麼不願意“把Levent扔到車輪底下”。 Bubeck對此同樣感到不解。 他告訴《紐約時報》，OpenAI此前完成其他數學證明後，也曾與外部數學家達成過類似合作安排，因此他對Buckmaster拒絕合作的反應感到驚訝。 至於“毀掉職業生涯”的警告，Bubeck給出的語境是： Buckmaster表示，只要OpenAI公佈證明，就會立即向媒體提出一系列指控。 他真正想問的是，為什麼要用未經證實的指控冒險損害自己的職業生涯。 Bubeck承認這是“極其糟糕的措辭”，稱自己當場收回並道歉。 但Buckmaster顯然沒有感受到其中的“善意”。 週日，他把紐約大學的辦公室變成了一間臨時“作戰室” ： 黑板上寫滿事件時間線，幾名同事坐在旁邊，和他一起討論該怎麼應對。 他還給普林斯頓高等研究院數學家Peter Sarnak打了電話。Sarnak聽完雙方提出的條件後表示： 這種討價還價，我從來沒有聽說過。 他同時稱讚Buckmaster“按照數學家的方式行事”。 週一接近午夜，Buckmaster倉促公開了三篇尚未來得及充分潤色的論文，以及一份1870詞的事件說明。 直到凌晨2點30分，他才離開辦公室回家。 幾個小時後，OpenAI正式宣佈完成納維-斯托克斯證明。 而這場爭議真正刺痛數學家的，也許還不只是資料。 Buckmaster認為， 在爭吵中被忽略的，是人類數學家為這次突破鋪出的道路 。 幾年前，西班牙數學家Diego Córdoba和Luis Martínez-Zoroa提出了一套攻擊相關流體方程的新策略： 通過一連串精確的外力“踢擊”，不斷將流體推向極端狀態，最終逼出速度趨近無窮大的奇點。 Buckmaster負責設定問題，Alpöge將問題輸入Anthropic的模型。 兩人再根據模型輸出不斷反饋、修正，逐步解決更複雜的方程。 Buckmaster因此強調： 主要的智力功勞應該歸於Luis和Diego 。 按照過去的研究節奏，這套方法本可以由不同數學家繼續接力，或許再用十年時間走到納維-斯托克斯。 但現在，OpenAI調動上萬個Agent，把這段路壓縮到了幾天。 一邊是前人用幾年時間提出核心策略，另一邊是AI用海量算力完成最後衝刺。 那麼，這項突破究竟應該算誰的？ 這個問題還沒有答案。 但我們能看到的是，OpenAI已經開始刷下一道了。。。 下一道可能是霍奇猜想，模型或叫Aeon 最新爆料稱，OpenAI已經把下一個目標鎖定在了 霍奇猜想 。 早在納維-斯托克斯結果公佈前，Epoch AI數學負責人Elliot Glazer梳理當時混亂的訊息源時，就提到一名數學教授從所謂“可信渠道”聽到： 被攻克的不是納維-斯托克斯，而是霍奇猜想 。 當時這條訊息被視為傳聞中的傳聞。 如今OpenAI確認又在一道千禧年難題上取得“實質性進展”，這條舊線索也被重新翻了出來。 雖然是不是還有待兩說，但種種傳聞已經讓它成為目前呼聲最高的答案。 那麼，霍奇猜想到底在猜什麼？ 簡單來說，它試圖在數學的兩個世界之間搭一座橋。 一個是拓撲學，關注高維空間整體上有多少個“洞”。 另一個是代數幾何，研究由多項式方程刻畫出來的幾何形狀。 霍奇猜想認為，在一類特定的複雜幾何空間中，那些由拓撲學發現的特殊“洞”，並不是憑空存在的，它們背後應該都能找到由代數方程構成的幾何結構。換句話說： 一個空間裡看不見、摸不著的拓撲特徵，背後應該存在可以用方程寫出來的“骨架” 。 這個猜想由英國數學家William Hodge在20世紀提出，後來被列入七大千禧年大獎難題。它連線了拓撲學、復幾何與代數幾何，也是現代數學最核心、最難啃的問題之一。 而可能挑戰它的，仍是那個沒有正式名字的OpenAI內部模型 。 OpenAI目前只透露，該模型從8月28日開始訓練，數學能力已經顯著超過GPT-6 Astra，甚至在納維-斯托克斯專案進行期間，它還沒有結束訓練。 外界則傳言，它的代號可能是 Aeon ，但這一名稱尚未獲得OpenAI證實。 就是這個“邊訓練、邊刷題”的模型，被接入一個由上萬個Agent組成的系統，同時嘗試多道尚未解決的千禧年難題。 OpenAI披露，整輪測試產生了490萬條Agent訊息和約3000億個輸出Token，其中僅納維-斯托克斯一題，就動用了約1萬個並行Agent，產生270萬條訊息，消耗約1300億個輸出Token。 從Agent啟動到找到解法，只用了88個小時，隨後GPT-6 Astra又花費17個小時完成Lean形式化和驗證。 納維-斯托克斯，只是這套暴力解題系統公開交出的第一張答卷。 現在，第二道題也已經在路上了。 OpenAI和Anthropic，已經把世紀猜想當測試集刷了 把最近半個月的訊息放在一起看，會發現這並不是一次偶然的數學突破： 更像是一場被傳聞點燃、迅速升級的AI刷題競賽 。 事件的主角當然是OpenAI和Anthropic這對宿敵，雙方瞄準的還都是千禧年難題這種數學界的“終極Boss”。 （七道千禧年難題中，此前只有龐加萊猜想獲得正式解決，如果OpenAI的納維-斯托克斯證明最終通過審查，那就還剩五道了。） 這場大戰究竟有多誇張，一張表格看明白： △圖片由AI生成 最興奮的當然是，許多困擾人類幾十年甚至上百年的問題，可能會被快速推進。 但對數學家而言，另一面也很真實： 他們提出問題、積累路線、把未公開草稿交給AI工具，最後卻可能發現，工具背後的公司正在與自己搶跑。 Buckmaster說， 他並不在意100萬美元獎金，只是熱愛數學，想成為這段歷史的一部分 。 如今，他確實進了歷史，只是方式和他想的完全不一樣。 面對《紐約時報》，這位數學家說： 與一家萬億美元公司對抗，非常可怕。 我們都害怕OpenAI。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 OpenAI 一水 ECCV上，頂尖學者們開始研究如何讓AI做生意了 2026-09-10 title: 吹爆開源！RunningHub讓MiniMax H3滿血提速12倍，本地部署照樣起飛
abstract: 吹爆開源！RunningHub讓MiniMax H3滿血提速12倍，本地部署照樣起飛 聞樂 2026-09-11 08:55:01 來源： 量子位 15秒影片，50秒出片 聞樂 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI MiniMax H3是真強也是真火啊。 開源還能打，在AI影片圈也算是獨一份了。 模型底座強成這樣，開發者們自然也閒不住，開始琢磨怎麼把它玩得更爽。 所以MiniMax前腳剛把H3開源，後腳各種工作流、ComfyUI節點、垂直最佳化玩法就已經冒了出來。 這不，一站式AIGC創作平臺 RunningHub 就盯上了一個大家都特《急急急》的事兒： 讓H3跑快點。 咋說呢，模型越好用人越忍不住多抽幾次，結果一抽一個大等待。 靈感一上頭，創意改起來只要十幾秒，下一版都已經在腦子裡剪完了，結果螢幕上的這一版還在轉…… 於是乎，RunningHub乾脆給H3踩了腳油門，直接朝著等待時間砍了一刀。 同樣生成5秒、1344×768的影片，在4張RTX 6000D上，原始BF16 50步方案耗時 348.8秒，差不多6分鐘 。 RunningHub H3 Lightning完整加速之後，只需要 28.7秒 。 好傢伙，前後約 12倍提速 ，生成耗時減少約92%，卻依舊能保留BF16數值精度。 現在，RunningHub已經把整套玩法放GitHub上開源了，任何創作者都能開箱即用！ （https://github.com/RH-RunningHub/MiniMax-H3-MultiGPU-Lightning/） 快12倍的H3是啥體驗 不光是5秒影片，就算是15秒、雙參考圖，RunningHub H3 Lightning依舊能給你猛猛提速。 在8張RTX 6000D環境下，讓H3做一個15秒、解析度768×1344的影片，純文字生成大約需要48秒、雙參考圖生成約73秒。 也就是說，一條15秒的圖生影片，可以打進 “1分鐘出結果” 這個時間尺度了。 而且在RunningHub H3 Lightning這兒，AI加速可不等於質量劣化。 整套加速方案還全程保留BF16滿血精度，沒有走降精度換速度的“捷徑”。 一個本來就已經很能打的模型，又被狠狠優化了一波，咱必須得體驗一把！ 我先試了一個5秒、768P的文生影片，直接來個大動作。 場景放在沙漠，一個女越野摩托車手原地起步，隨後高速衝上沙丘，騰空、落地，再接一個大幅甩尾。 嫌這還不夠，我又給鏡頭加了點活兒。 先低機位側面追車，隨後繞到正面倒退跟拍，最後讓摩托直接從鏡頭旁邊衝過去。 從點選生成到出片的實際用時約為 30s ，人、車、沙塵的運動邏輯挺連貫。 落地的時候車身有明顯的下沉和回彈，騎手的重心也跟著往下壓了一下，還有塵土的飛揚看著也挺真實。 我預設的機位也都安排妥了。 影片地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/bygc8puWmTmN2KSt7otkwA 其實，除了畫面質量高之外我最大的感受是，等待間隙我甚至都沒刷完一個某音影片…… 確實是絲滑。 不過5秒還是短，咱還得上強度。 再試試15秒的圖生影片，這次我餵了一張吉卜力風格的參考圖。 △圖片AI生成 原本是一人一狗背對著鏡頭坐在草地上，現在咱讓他倆跑起來。 少年從草地上起身，直接向山坡前方奔跑；金毛也得跟著起來，一邊跑一邊跳；少年中途還要張開雙臂、轉身繼續跑。 鏡頭從背後推進，再切到側面跟拍，最後拉遠，把整個山谷重新帶進畫面。 15秒長影片的生成時間就比較久了，從點選到出片大概 88秒 。 從坐著到起身，再到邁步加速，動作之間有比較明顯的銜接；金毛也沒有淪為一張跟著人物平移的貼紙，自己完成了起身、奔跑和跳躍。 更關鍵的是，15秒跑下來，這一人一狗還基本是原來那一人一狗。 少年的黃色外套、藍色褲子、黑色頭髮這些主要特徵一直都在，金毛的體型和毛色也沒有跑到後半段突然換了個品種。 而且鏡頭轉完一圈後，遠處的湖泊和夕陽依舊在畫面中。 影片地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/bygc8puWmTmN2KSt7otkwA 當然了，你要是真盯著看也還是能挑出毛病。狗在快速跳躍時，四肢動作偶爾會有點“硬”，但是倒也不會特別出戲。 本來打算收工了，我又突然冒出來一個想法，晴天不要了，給我下雨。 沒錯咱創作的時候靈感就是嘎嘎跳躍！ 少年得站起來撐傘，在草地上跑，再突然停下轉一圈；金毛繼續繞著他跑，還得從旁邊跳過去。 與此同時，原來的遠山和湖泊還得留住。 二次創作的時間變短了，也就50秒左右，最後畫面遠處還出現了一抹彩虹～ 影片地址：https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/bygc8puWmTmN2KSt7otkwA 之前想改個人物、場景、鏡頭啥的，動手之前可能會考慮考慮值不值得再等很長時間。 現在不用愁了，有了靈感就能快速出片。 對很多創作者來說，創意落地、試錯的時間成本都降低了，也不用因為漫長等待就砍掉很多一閃而過的想法。 那麼問題來了， 不降BF16精度，也不開掛頂級資料中心算力，RunningHub摳出來的時間，到底是從哪兒省出來的？ 人人都能用，本地可部署 快，自然是用工程摳出來的，解法是很工整的三刀—— 先看看哪裡算得太多，再看看哪裡算得太慢，最後看看幾張GPU之間有沒有時間浪費在“互相等”上。 第一刀，先從模型本身動手，讓H3少算一點。 影片生成不是模型看完Prompt，啪一下就直接把最終畫面吐出來。 它需要一輪一輪地把畫面“想”出來。 把文字或者圖片變成影片需要經過多輪計算，畫面才會逐漸從噪聲中成形，這個輪次叫生成步數。 原始H3推理預設50步，每一步背後都有一輪實打實的計算，步數越多，GPU自然就得幹得越久。 RunningHub做的第一件事，就是引入 自研的RH後訓練加速模型 。 簡單點說就是讓H3經過後訓練之後，學會用更少的步數把影片做出來，還得在不丟畫質的前提下完成。 這一步的效果已經相當明顯。 同樣使用4張RTX 6000D生成5秒影片，換成RH後訓練加速模型的9步測試方案之後，時間直接縮短到了43秒。 第一刀下去，已經提速了8倍。 順便說一句，RunningHub的推薦配置是預設4步； 遇到快速運動、大幅動作這類難任務可以切到8步，快還是穩，咱創作者自己來決定。 做到43秒，按理說已經挺猛了，但RunningHub顯然還嫌慢。 模型雖然少算了，可剩下這些必須完成的計算，總不能就這麼放著吧。 RunningHub接著想解決的是，剩下這些必須完成的計算，還有沒有地方能繼續省時間？ 於是第二刀開始往執行層裡砍。 這次一口氣上了三個技術組合， SageAttention2、Cache-DiT和torch.compile 。 SageAttention2盯的是 注意力計算 。 影片模型每生成一段內容，都需要處理大量畫面元素之間的關係。 誰和誰相關、前後畫面怎麼聯絡、不同資訊怎麼共同影響最終結果，這些注意力計算本身就是推理過程中相當吃算力的一環。 SageAttention2要做的就是讓這塊核心計算執行得更高效。 Cache-DiT則開始盯著 重複勞動 。 影片生成前後多個計算步驟之間存在可以複用的資訊，如果有些中間結果已經算過，後面的步驟就沒必要每次都從頭再來。 能快取的快取，能複用的複用，把重複工作減下來，時間自然還能繼續往下擠。 最後還有torch.compile，它會對計算過程進行 編譯最佳化 ，讓GPU執行這些操作時更加順暢，減少一些原本零散的排程和執行開銷。 當RH後訓練加速模型和這些運算元、快取、編譯最佳化疊到一起，該跑快的跑快，該複用的複用，該捋順的捋順，剛才壓到43秒的生成過程又被繼續壓到了28.7秒。 但這還沒完，H3這種影片模型真跑起來，往往不會只讓一張GPU單打獨鬥。 多張卡一起幹活，新的問題就又來了。 卡多，不等於一定快 。這和多人一起幹活其實挺像的。 八個人當然比一個人手多，可如果任務分配不合適，每個人剛乾兩下就要停下來等別人遞東西，A等B，B等C，最後時間全耗在互相交接上。 多卡推理也是類似的道理。 GPU之間需要不斷交換資料，而在沒有NVLink高速互聯、主要依靠PCIe通訊的環境裡，卡間通訊的成本尤其不能忽略。 RunningHub這次專門針對這種環境，把不同的多卡並行方式拉出來重新測了一遍，最後選中的組合是 TP2＋Ulysses4 。 TP負責從張量計算層面拆任務，Ulysses則進一步從序列維度做並行。 在8張RTX 6000D、PCIe連線且沒有NVLink的環境下，TP2＋Ulysses4相比TP4＋Ulysses2， 速度快約12%，同時減少約14GiB視訊記憶體佔用 。 所以從整體技術路徑來看，這套工程棧基本就是沿著推理鏈路一路摳時間： RH後訓練加速模型先把需要完成的計算量壓下來； SageAttention2、Cache-DiT和torch.compile繼續提高剩餘計算的執行效率； 到了多卡層面，再用TP2＋Ulysses4減少通訊和資源上的浪費； 最後，RunningHub把這些方法全部整合進SGLang multimodal_gen推理引擎，由它把模型生成、多卡協同和各種加速元件真正組織到一起。 現在AI行業的各種效能數字已經卷得飛起，只要捨得堆頂級GPU、高速互聯和資料中心，把模型跑得飛快並不稀奇。 可真正想本地部署開源影片模型的創作者、工作室和中小團隊要問了： 我手裡的機器，能不能跑出這個速度？ RunningHub：必須能。 H3 Lightning特意繞開了“超能力解法”，針對的就是無NVLink的PCIe多卡環境，RTX 6000D也是公開可購買的專業GPU規格。 也就是說，RunningHub從一開始針對性最佳化的，就是一種更貼近工作室和企業團隊實際部署的多卡環境。 當然了，如果你的預算沒上限，用B300的卡配合這個方式，出片速度能直接提升至秒級。 從環境安裝、模型下載，到服務啟動和推理測試，H3 Lightning整個本地部署流程都公開了。 開發者也可以結合公開的社群加速LoRA，再配上前面提到的注意力最佳化、計算快取和多卡並行，在自己的機器上重新跑一遍。 到底要幾張卡、怎麼調參數、速度和畫質怎麼取捨，都可以圍繞自己的業務適配。 當然了，有裝置的團隊可以照著開源方案自己部署； 沒有多卡伺服器、不想研究環境配置的創作者， 直接在RunningHub上點開H3 Lightning也能用 。 頂級算力被壟斷，RunningHub選了創作者夠得著的那條路 當一個足夠強的開源模型出來之後，圍繞它其實會出現很多“二創”。 有人會拿開源底座繼續做後訓練，把最佳化後的能力跑在頂級資料中心叢集上，再封裝成API提供給使用者。 使用者不需要關心背後的GPU和工程最佳化，按呼叫付費就能直接獲得結果，這當然是一種很成熟的商業路徑。 另一邊，也會有人選擇 把最佳化繼續留在開源生態裡 —— 開發者自己擁有硬體、自己部署模型，圍繞自己的工作流繼續改，最佳化方法又能被下一批開發者拿去復現和迭代。 RunningHub這次明顯更偏向後者。 而且，這已經不是它第一次圍著H3這麼幹了。 H3剛開源的時候，RunningHub首先做的是 接入 。 模型出來之後，平臺第一時間把它接進來，讓創作者不用先研究一大堆部署問題，就可以上手嘗試新模型。 隨後，它又 參與生態共建 ，把全套ComfyUI節點開源。 這一下，開發者能玩的更多了。 有人拿H3做電商內容，有人拿去做 短劇、漫劇 ，有人研究 聲音克隆、動作克隆和音訊驅動 ，還有人繼續把自己的玩法封裝成新的工作流。 比如，創作者@魅力創意直接盯上了電商影片。 TA釋出的MiniMax H3·電商多參生影片工作流，只需要把商品、模特、場景一股腦塞進去，再簡單說說賣點—— H3就能自己琢磨人物該在哪兒、商品怎麼露出、場景怎麼搭，最後直接給你一條完整電商廣告。 還有創作者@艾橘溪整的音訊驅動數字人說話唱歌工作流。 上傳一張人物圖片，再扔進去一段音訊，原本靜止的人物就能秒變數字人開口營業。 不管是說話還是唱歌，口型和節奏都能同步對上。 還有今年超火的漫劇，創作者@qwlulnpi也搬出了新創意。 把分鏡圖、指令碼、音訊一次性丟進去就能拿到有畫面有聲音的完整成片。 多少有點“素材備齊，一把梭哈”的流水線味兒了。 這還只是RunningHub上冒出來的一小撮玩法。 自打H3上線以來，RunningHub平臺上已經有上千名創作者，圍繞它開源了近萬條創意工作流。 其實這也是開源模型的樂趣，一個人解決一點問題，最後整個生態能用的東西就越來越多。 而H3 Lightning相當於RunningHub再進一步，開始把自己積累的工程能力反過來貢獻給H3，直接解決推理效率的問題。 如果只看RunningHub，一個AIGC創作平臺突然跑去研究後訓練、運算元最佳化和多卡並行，多少有點跨界。 但把它放回母公司 海馬雲 過去十多年的技術演進裡，這事兒其實順理成章。 海馬雲2014年成立，過去十多年長期和GPU、高效能內容打交道。 那個時候，行業面對的問題還不是“AI大模型怎麼推理”。 當時的核心矛盾是遊戲、圖形、高效能數字內容體量越來越大，如何讓這些負載穩定、高速地執行起來。 GPU容器排程、圖形虛擬化、即時流媒體、大規模雲渲染，海馬雲的整套能力體系都是圍繞這個目標打磨的。 時至今日，海馬雲已經在國內建設60餘個邊緣節點，支撐超過2000萬月活使用者的智算服務。 到了生成式AI時代，需要被高效排程的計算物件發生了變化。 除了遊戲、圖形和高效能數字內容，現在還加入了大模型，以及模型驅動的內容生成。 於是海馬雲面對的命題也隨之從「高效能內容怎麼跑」，進一步轉向了「AI能力如何呼叫，又如何高效落地」。 計算物件從雲渲染到AI推理，但這也恰好讓海馬雲這家 原生AI公司 十餘年的技術積累有了更大的發揮場景。 所以RunningHub並不算“跨界”做模型加速。 RunningHub H3 Lightning，是海馬雲 「GPU工程能力」 在AI時代的一個新落點，補齊的也是開源模型從權重到生產力之間缺失的環節。 過去一年，開源模型越來越多，真正稀缺的是： 誰能在模型開源之後，最快把它接進真實環境、最佳化到生產可用，再把這些能力持續回饋給社群。 模型開源，RunningHub平臺完成接入，創作者「能直接用」了； 開放ComfyUI節點與工作流，創作者「能玩的花樣」多了； 而H3 Lightning推理最佳化，則是在模型跑通之後，繼續攻克速度、成本與硬體門檻，把單次試玩的內容生成，升級為可穩定複用的批次生產力。 RunningHub就是這樣一個 生態反哺者 。 咱普通創作者也算是跟著吃上細糠了～ GitHub倉庫：https://github.com/RH-RunningHub/MiniMax-H3-MultiGPU-Lightning/ 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 AIGC RunningHub 海馬雲 聞樂 新版GPT Image 2.5已經能偽造GPT-6釋出會了 2026-09-04 剛剛，GPT-6正式釋出！OpenAI：歡迎來到AGI時代 2026-09-04 Coding不再是程式設計師專屬！阿里Qoder這波有點絕 2026-08-29 AI4S開始進入「專案時代」：紫東太初把AI從做Task推向做Project 2026-08-25 相關閱讀

title: Together AI expands fine-tuning service with more models, live metrics, and finer controls
abstract: Turning an open-weight model into a high-performing model for your task takes a sequence of well-measured experiments. Teams need to understand what the model will train on, follow how each run is progressing, adjust the training recipe, and identify which checkpoint performs best. Today, we're expanding Together Fine-Tuning across that workflow. This release adds support for the latest open-weight models, live experiment tracking, finer controls over training and data processing, and lower prices on selected models. You can also inspect and validate a dataset before training, compare runs while they are in flight, and stop when validation loss plateaus. New models New open-weight models are arriving at an unprecedented pace, with nearly every release raising the bar for quality, efficiency, or both. Teams want to bring these advances into production quickly, without spending weeks on the technical challenges of each new architecture. For tasks that need frontier performance, you can turn to the largest and strongest models such as GLM-5.3 and Kimi K2.7. For example, GLM-5.3 scores 88.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, within one point of the leading proprietary models. Other teams prioritize performance and costs, choosing models such as Qwen 3.8-27B or Gemma 4. For local and on-device applications, the Qwen 3.5 family offers options ranging from 0.8B to 9B parameters. Together Fine-Tuning supports all these models across a wide range of scales, with leading optimizations across systems and algorithms built in. Submit a training job, and we handle the architecture-specific complexity behind the scenes. The latest additions include: GLM 5.3 GLM-5.2 GLM-5.1 DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 DeepSeek-V4-Flash Kimi K2.7-Code Kimi K2.6 Qwen 3.8-27B Qwen 3.6-35B-A3B Qwen 3.6-27B Qwen 3.5-27B Qwen 3.5-9B Qwen 3.5-4B Qwen 3.5-2B Qwen 3.5-0.8B Gemma 4-31B Gemma 4-26B-A4B View the full list of supported models along with their context lengths in our documentation. Experiment tracking The sooner a run's trajectory is visible, the sooner the next decision can be made - adjust the data, change the hyperparameters, or let it finish. Fine-tuning jobs now record metrics at every training and evaluation step and expose them directly through the Together API, CLI, and UI dashboard. Metrics, job status, and artifacts stay in one place, so you can remain on the same platform for the entire journey of model development. Every run captures the core training signals: loss, gradient norm, learning rate. When you add a validation set, the evaluation loss and metrics will be tracked alongside training metrics. In the dashboard, every job gets a Metrics tab with curves that update while the run is still in flight - and you can select several jobs and chart them together on one set of axes, so a sweep reads as a single picture instead of a dozen browser tabs. You can also do the same via our Python SDK: one command, curve in the terminal, no context switch. The API returns the underlying series - every recorded step, filtered by range or downsampled. This way, you can pull metrics into a notebook, your internal dashboards you already have, or any other destination. See more details in our documentation. More controls over training Expert LoRA In a Mixture-of-Experts model, over 90% of the parameters, and most of what the model actually knows , live in the expert layers. Standard LoRA fine-tuning never touches them: adapters attach to attention while the experts stay frozen. You can now put LoRA adapters on the experts themselves, so your job can train the layers where the knowledge lives. The difference shows up wherever a task needs the model to learn something genuinely new. We taught models 200 invented facts (so the base models know none of them): adapters that include the expert layers recalled up to 89% of the new knowledge, while attention-only adapters topped out at 15% on the same model. They also kept more of the model's existing knowledge and won MMLU-Pro outright, 75.3% to 71.5%. The training dynamics explain the gap: with attention-only adapters, a growing share of routed experts simply falls out of use during fine-tuning, while expert adapters keep the whole mixture engaged. Enabling expert adapters is simple: just add the expert modules to lora_trainable_modules . The rest of the fine-tuning workflow remains the same as it does for any other LoRA job . Early stopping Fine-tuning jobs can now automatically finish when they stop improving. That means you get the best model, not just the last one, and you don't pay for training that no longer helps. Enable early stopping, provide a validation set, and we'll watch your validation loss at every evaluation. When the curve plateaus, we halt the run, keep the checkpoint with the best validation loss as your final model, and automatically refund every training step you didn't use. Patience, sensitivity to small improvements, and warmup are all tunable when you want finer control. The full parameter reference is in the docs . Arbitrary batch size support Some jobs need batch sizes that can't fit in GPU memory: long sequences, large models or a recipe tuned for a big global batch. You can now train with whatever effective batch size you want regardless of what fits in a single pass. Set gradient_accumulation_steps and gradients accumulate across micro-batches before each optimizer update, giving an effective batch of batch_size x gradient_accumulation_steps. Details in the docs . Price reductions At Together, we believe that intelligence should be abundant, and we leverage all available systems and algorithmic optimizations to provide the most value to our customers. We continue optimizing our training stack and want to transfer any cost reductions to users. Hence, we are dropping the prices of training for most of the models we support, with savings starting from 30% and reaching 70% for models such as the gpt-oss series. Here are some of the price changes for training LoRA adapters per 1 million tokens: Model Old SFT New SFT Old DPO New DPO Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B 0.48 0.34 1.20 0.84 Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B 1.50 1.05 3.75 2.62 google/gemma-4-31B-it 1.50 1.05 3.75 2.62 openai/gpt-oss-120b 5.00 2.50 12.50 6.25 openai/gpt-oss-20b 1.50 0.40 3.75 1.00 The full pricing table is available on our pricing page . Case study: How Adaption automates training for open models up to 1T on Together Adaption is a frontier AI research company building intelligence that continuously learns, evolving through live data and environments rather than static training and costly retraining cycles. Its research spans three pillars: Adaptive Data, which shapes data at scale Adaptive Intelligence, which evolves models across industries and languages Adaptive Interfaces, which reimagines human-AI interaction AutoScientist, part of Adaptive Intelligence, automates the full research loop behind model training. Where Adaptive Data shapes the inputs, AutoScientist shapes the model itself: you set the outcome, and the loop searches training recipes, optimizes the data, trains, and evaluates, cycling through all four rather than defaulting to generic hyperparameters. It refines its choices with every run until quality converges on your objective. It supports both LoRA and full fine-tuning across leading open models up to 1T parameters, with training powered by Together's fine-tuning platform and evaluation run on Together's dedicated endpoints. The result is a closed loop that keeps improving a model, without the manual effort or retraining costs that would otherwise demand it. "We have partnered with Together to run Adaption's AutoScientist full self-improvement training loop at up to 1 trillion parameter models. It allows us to provide companies around the world with self-improving intelligence at scale with tooling that reliably delivers.

title: Health Plans: Your BI Tells You MLR Moved. Can Your AI Tell You Why?
abstract: A health plan CFO closes the month after the usual round of extracts, spreadsheets, and manual reconciliation, and sees the financials are behind budget on a higher-than-expected medical loss ratio (MLR). A BI dashboard can surface the variance quickly. But “MLR is up” isn’t really the answer. It’s the beginning of the question. Which line of business or market is driving it? Are claim costs up and, if so, due to utilization, unit cost, or service mix? Was a group or product mispriced? Did population morbidity change? And what corrective action can be taken? The real opportunity for AI in payer finance isn't identifying the variance. It's understanding what caused it and what to do about it. AI transformation in finance results in three things changing at once. Answers arrive in minutes instead of a reporting cycle. Leaders double-click on their own, without a canned report or waiting on an analyst. AI can look past claims, revenue, and membership to clinical information, quality measures, and risk scores, reading all of it at the same time to assess what is driving the variance. That work was never practical when the expertise for both the data and the subject matter was siloed. The challenge then becomes whether AI can understand enough about a health plan’s data and business for finance to trust and act on its insights. That’s where Databricks and Abacus come together. Databricks provides the data and AI capabilities that let organizations interact with governed enterprise data in new ways. Abacus brings the payer-specific data foundation, business context, and operational knowledge those capabilities need when the questions involve healthcare finance. For years, business intelligence worked by anticipating the questions someone would want to ask. Teams built reports. Analysts created dashboards. Executives reviewed the metrics someone had decided belonged on the page. When a number moved, figuring out why meant leaving the dashboard, finding the right analyst or team to investigate, pulling another report or reconciling multiple systems of record. And every answer left something behind: another report to run, another dashboard to build and maintain. Each one was already stale by the time the next question arrived. More work for the team and diminishing returns. Conversational AI changes that interaction model. Instead of stopping at what a dashboard was designed to show, a finance leader can ask a question in plain language, get an answer, and follow it with another question based on what they just learned. The experience starts to look less like navigating reports and more like investigating the business. What really breaks down is the barrier between two kinds of expertise. The executive knows the business and owns the decision-making but cannot query the data; the analyst knows the data, where it lives, how it is structured, how to manipulate it, but not always which question matters. AI collapses that handoff: the person who needs the answer can now ask for it directly. But the quality of that conversation depends on what the AI understands underneath it. For years, the data modernization question was largely about access: can we bring claims, membership, provider, contract, clinical, and financial data together so people can use it? That remains essential, but AI adds another requirement . It needs to understand what that data means. Consider the metric of MLR, the share of premium revenue spent on medical care for a plan’s members. Easy to define, hard to calculate. Claims and premiums come on different structures and different timelines, and “medical” expense is really a stack of components, including medical claims, pharmacy claims and rebates, incurred but not reported (IBNR), payment integrity recoveries, risk adjustment transfers, provider settlements, and more. Then it has to be cut by line of business, market, or product, and defining those cohorts takes business logic that never comes out of the box. Without that context, an AI system can have access to enormous amounts of data and still not produce adequate insights. Much of this business context has traditionally lived in different places: For AI to answer finance questions reliably, more of that context has to become explicit, consistent, and reusable. That is why a payer-specific data foundation matters. Health plan data does not arrive neatly organized around the questions executives want to ask. Claims, eligibility, provider, contract, clinical, and financial information come from different systems, in different formats, with different relationships and timing. Before AI can reason across it effectively, the data has to be connected and organized in a way that reflects how a health plan operates. Abacus provides that payer-specific foundation: bringing healthcare data together in a consistent structure and adding the business context needed to understand the relationships among members, claims, providers, contracts, clinical information, and financial measures. Even on the same underlying data, the “same” metric is often defined differently depending on who is calculating it. One version lands in the CFO’s monthly reporting package, while another shows up in an ad hoc analytics request, and eventually someone has to reconcile them. AI does not solve that problem on its own. Without consistent definitions, it amplifies it. For finance leaders, the issue isn't simply accuracy. It's confidence that the answer reflects how the business operates. The same definitions that let finance, actuarial, and operations teams work from a consistent view of performance also give AI the context it needs to interpret a question correctly. The goal isn’t simply one place where the data lives; it’s a consistent understanding of what the data means wherever it is used, whether an executive is asking conversationally or an analyst is producing a traditional report. Go back to the CFO. MLR is above budget. Where? What’s driving it? Which populations, services, or providers account for the change? And what should the organization do next? Each question requires more context than the one before it. The first needs a financial measure and a budget comparison. The second needs the components underneath the variance. The third crosses claims, membership, provider, contract, and care management data. By the fourth, the conversation has moved from financial reporting into operations. That’s why the real opportunity isn’t a better way to display a KPI. It’s a connected path from executive signal to operational double-clicks, one finance can walk without repeatedly handing the problem back to analysts to reconcile another set of reports or data points. The AI doesn’t replace the judgment about what the organization should do; it shortens the distance between seeing that something changed and understanding it well enough to act. Without the back-and-forth, each iteration is faster, and faster iteration raises the value of the decision itself: care management activities start sooner, emerging trends get priced in earlier, and corrective action happens while it can still change the outcome. MLR is a useful example because it sits at the intersection of finance and operations, but the underlying architecture isn’t specific to MLR. The same connected payer data and business context can support questions across payment integrity, total cost of care, risk adjustment, quality, and provider performance. That changes how health plans can think about AI investment. The alternative is a collection of disconnected AI use cases, each built around its own data, its own definitions, and its own view of the business. It’s the same fragmentation health plans have spent years trying to eliminate, only with an AI interface on top. A common payer intelligence foundation creates a different path: get the underlying data and context right once, then reuse it as new questions, workflows, and AI experiences emerge.

title: Unify your marketing data with Lakeflow Connect
abstract: This is the first post in a new series exploring how Lakeflow Connect brings fully managed data ingestion to every line of business. Each post focuses on a specific domain, showing you how to unify scattered data sources with native connectors and activate that foundation for downstream workloads — from reporting dashboards to conversational analytics with Databricks Genie . We are kicking things off with the most notoriously fragmented stack of all: Customer 360. Lakeflow Connect provides a comprehensive suite of fully managed native connectors across SaaS applications, databases, and file sources that ingest your data directly into the Databricks Platform . Each connector can be set up via a point-and-click UI or a simple API. From there, your data is incrementally ingested as governed, managed tables in Unity Catalog , with no infrastructure for you to provision, manage, or scale. Prioritized by customer demand, Lakeflow Connect’s ingestion connectors span every line of business, including Productivity, Operations, Finance, and — perhaps the most fragmented of them all — Customer 360. The modern marketing stack is a sprawl of ad platforms, analytics tools, and CRMs, each capturing only a slice of the customer. Painting a full picture has historically required a patchwork of custom ingestion pipelines and brittle scripts that data teams must both build and maintain. This drains engineering resources and slows down marketing analysts, who need answers fast: which campaigns actually drive retention? Which customers are about to churn? Lakeflow Connect resolves this by providing built-in connectors to ingest seamlessly from every stage of the customer journey: With this breadth of martech connectors, Lakeflow Connect becomes the critical ingestion engine that powers a complete customer 360, without the integration bottlenecks that traditionally slow teams down. From there, every report lands as a consistent, governed Unity Catalog table, ready for downstream analysis. title: Unifying governance across engines and catalogs in the Open Lakehouse
abstract: In our previous posts, we showed how open table formats, open APIs and unified governance are coming together to complete the Open Lakehouse vision . We also introduced cross-engine attribute-based access control , which allows policies defined in Unity Catalog to be enforced consistently when external engines access governed data. Now, that vision is beginning to materialize in the open. The Apache Iceberg™ community recently advanced two important additions to the Iceberg REST Catalog: read restrictions and catalog labels . Together, they address two distinct challenges: delegating enforcement to an external engine and making governance context portable across catalogs. In this post we will take a closer look at both new additions to the spec: how they work, key challenges they address, future opportunities for innovation, and when to use them. Read restrictions address a common engine-to-catalog scenario: an organization governs data in one catalog and wants to query it from various engines or tools. For any governed query, three things must happen: When data is accessed from an engine, these responsibilities can be divided in two ways. With centralized enforcement , all three steps remain within the catalog’s environment. For example, Databricks implements fine-grained access control on dedicated compute by transparently routing queries through a secure filtering fleet. And Unity Catalog’s Cross-engine ABAC feature extends this governance to other engines by putting the filtering fleet behind the Iceberg REST catalog scan/plan APIs to sanitize data before an external engine such as Spark 1 or DuckDB processes the result. With delegated enforcement, the catalog receives the requesting identity and evaluates policy, then returns the resulting row and column restrictions to an engine it trusts to enforce them. Here, trust means that the catalog can rely on the engine to enforce the restrictions and prevent users from bypassing them. Engines such as Spark and DuckDB are untrusted when users control the runtime because those users can execute arbitrary code or access the underlying data directly. A securely configured Trino deployment is an example of a trusted engine because it provides native enforcement for row filters and column masks. Delegated enforcement requires a common contract between the catalog and engine. The Iceberg community adopted read restrictions to provide that contract. When a reader loads a table through the Iceberg REST Catalog, the catalog evaluates the applicable policies for the requesting principal and request context. It can return required column-projection actions and row-filter expressions, and the trusted engine must apply those restrictions as it reads the table. Two design decisions are important to understanding the proposal’s current scope. First, the engine does not receive the policy as the administrator defined it. Instead, it receives the outcome for a particular principal, expressed as filtering or masking instructions that it must apply. This creates a common enforcement contract between the engine and catalog. The initial spec defines a bounded vocabulary: nine predefined column-projection actions and standardized row-filter expressions such as comparisons or set membership. Many real-world enterprise policies depend on subqueries, lookup tables or custom UDFs, which cannot be expressed within the read restrictions vocabulary. This has an important implication: policies can be represented only when the catalog can reduce their result to the vocabulary defined by the standard, otherwise you lose policy semantics. Second, the specification defines what a trusted engine must enforce, but not how the catalog establishes that trust. A claim from the client is not sufficient, so system administrators and implementations must use security mechanisms appropriate to their environment. Iceberg community discussions have considered mechanisms such as mTLS and OAuth, but trust ultimately remains outside the protocol ( Iceberg community discussion ). Read restrictions are best suited for direct engine-to-catalog access scenarios where the source catalog’s policies are simple and a trusted engine can enforce the resulting decision. Many implementation questions remain, such as how an engine securely propagates the end user’s identity and attributes, how a catalog distinguishes the user from the engine acting on the user’s behalf, and how credentials are bound to their intended recipient. As implementations emerge, we’re excited to collaborate with the Iceberg community to work through these challenges and evolve the standard. Catalog labels address a different scenario: governance across federated catalogs. Many enterprises now connect multiple catalogs, such as Unity Catalog, Snowflake, AWS Lake Formation and Google Cloud Knowledge Catalog, through federation and open APIs. This is more complex than an engine-to-catalog integration because each catalog serves its own users, applications, and engines through distinct identity models, policy languages, and semantics. Any unified governance solution that works at enterprise scale must: Catalog labels, recently adopted by the Iceberg community, is the first step towards this vision. Labels allow catalogs to exchange lightweight key-value metadata at the table and column level via Open APIs. Labels can indicate that a field contains PII, associate a dataset with a business domain, or provide semantic hints for AI models. Because the proposal is general, labels can support many use cases beyond access control, including discovery, ownership, cost attribution, AI context, and data quality. When a consuming catalog loads a table from a producing catalog via catalog federation, the producing catalog returns table and column-level labels. The consuming catalog then maps the labels into its own classifications, attributes or native tag model. It then evaluates access using its native identities and policies and enforces controls within its own runtime. For example, if a producing catalog labels an ssn column pii=ssn, the consuming catalog can apply a tag-based policy that masks columns carrying that label. Because policy enforcement remains local, the consuming catalog preserves the expressiveness of its native policies and avoids calling the producing catalog for each access decision. Each catalog also independently maintains its enforcement records and audit trail. It is worth keeping in mind that labels are opaque key-value pairs. The standard defines no shared semantics or stable identifiers, and lineage for labels does not extend beyond the source catalog. The consuming catalog receives only the resolved key and value, not whether the label was intended for discovery, access control, cost attribution, or another purpose. Labels therefore make metadata portable, but not its meaning; enterprises still need shared conventions or explicit mappings to interpret labels consistently. Catalog labels are best suited for catalog-to-catalog scenarios with federation between heterogeneous systems, where the consuming catalog has its own governance system and needs reusable context rather than a separate access decision for every user and request. The core idea is that governance and business context, like table metadata, should be open and portable through the Iceberg REST Catalog APIs. The right model depends on the destination: centralized enforcement for an untrusted engine, read restrictions for a trusted engine, and catalog labels for open metadata exchange when the destination is another catalog with its own governance system. title: Claude users found ways around safeguards for bioweapons research
abstract: Anthropic said it stopped multiple attempts by scientists this year to use its technology for research that could help develop biological weapons, as experts increasingly fear the threat that AI poses to public safety. The startup gave five examples of times actors “circumvented controls” and made other efforts to “obfuscate” the purpose of their research to dodge safeguards. The cases involved some users in nations that it prohibits from accessing its models, which include Russia, China, and Iran. “We hope that by sharing these examples, we spark a conversation within the AI industry and with governments about emerging biological risks and how best to counter them,” Anthropic said in a report about efforts to use its models for malicious activity. The case studies of possible biological misuse that the company provided included a researcher from an “unsupported region” who “spent weeks planning” experiments involving avian influenza with Claude, Anthropic’s AI model. The company said its safety filters restricted the work to its weakest models. It emphasized it could not be sure that the scientists in its examples intended to cause harm. The same information needed to create biological weapons could also be used to develop a vaccine. Anthropic said it had banned the accounts mentioned in the report, but it did not disclose the names of the research institutions or the nations where the incidents took place.

title: Jacob Coxon Warns of Human Extinction and Triggers a Preference Cascade
abstract: CEOs of major AI labs, and employees of major AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, often say they plan to build superintelligence soon, as in within a few years create AIs that are superior to humans at essentially all cognitive tasks. They often warn that such AIs might kill everyone. Or that AIs might cause mass unemployment, cause cyberattacks across the internet, enable mass surveillance or risk causing any number of other highly bad things. These warnings are consistently and directly against the interests of the labs. Yet the warnings have recently gotten a lot louder and more frequent. OpenAI has been practically screaming, for those with ears to listen, on many occasions. A series of events, over two months and especially the last week or so, including internal observations of the pace of progress at OpenAI and also Anthropic, have freaked out everyone involved quite a lot more than they were already freaked out. After all the events, plus statements by Dean Ball and Jakub Pachocki , we were already seeing the beginnings of a preference cascade. Then along came Jacob Coxon as the tipping point, and things took off. Jacob Coxon spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. He has come to realize that everyone involved is being wildly irresponsible. He warns us: They are racing straight to superintelligence and gambling with our lives. I agree with and strongly endorse his statement. If anything he sounds like an optimist. He’s asking you to consider what the next few years will actually feel like, which means he thinks you have a few years left. Jacob Coxon (former Anthropic and OpenAI, 160m+ views, September 8): I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below. Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing. The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger. A common response is “if they truly believe this, why are they still building it?” At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first – they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk. Accepting this race and entering the “endgame” is a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company’s Slack . Attempting to speedrun alignment should require extraordinary confidence that there are no better trajectories available. I am optimistic about the potential for coordination. Warning shots like the Hugging Face attack have made pacing agreements between U.S. labs more viable. I don’t feel like we’re on track to prevent a global race, which may require costly actions such as a temporary ban on improving model capabilities. If you are a lab researcher, I urge you to consider what the next few years will actually feel like. Do you want to kick off a superintelligent RL run without a rigorous understanding of its mind? Should you put your head down because “it’s happening anyway” – or take this moment to call for different conditions? Jacob Coxon (WSJ interview): We’re on track for a lot of the most aggressive of these scenarios where by the end of next year things could be out of control already. If you want Jacob Coxon’s full views, I recommend his interview with Wired’s Maxwell Zeff . This thread has extensive quotes . Here is Jacob Coxon doing a 5 minute interview with Anderson Cooper . He speaks well and plainly, and it is clear how much the events of the last two months have made it much easier to speak plainly to a civilian like Cooper about what is happening. Here is Jimmy Kimmel doing four minutes on this . He gets it. How is this not the top news story on every site, indeed. Yes, this is a common view, even if few have the courage to act. Alex Turner : I left Google DeepMind in June. Jacob is right: many researchers believe they are building something that could kill everyone on the planet. It was literally my day job to think about how to stop that. That tells you how bad Alex Turner thought DeepMind’s actions were with regard to the Department of War. His day job was that he got paid by Google to think about how to stop AI from killing everyone, and he felt morally obligated to quit in protest. Derek Thompson here writes about this as part of AI Safety Is Having a Moment . If you want to see the full list of lab employee quotes from the preference cascade, I compiled them into another post today . There was strong coverage of this, starting at the Wall Street Journal : Anthropic Researcher Quits Over ‘Out-of-Control’ AI Fears. I do worry there is an unfortunate second way to read that headline. Here is a sample of others, Astra can find many more: CNN: ‘Gambling with our lives’: Another AI employee quits over safety concerns FT: Anthropic researcher quits over AI labs ‘gambling with our lives’ Axios: Anthropic insiders warn AI could kill all humans . Fortune: Anthropic researcher resigns, warning AI companies are ‘gambling with our lives’ Fox Business: Anthropic researcher says AI has over 10% chance to ‘kill all humans’ BBC: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI ‘could kill all humans. ’ Jacob Coxon started this. Evan Hubinger had the other key Tweet that set this off: Evan Hubinger (Alignment Science Lead, Anthropic): Jacob [Coxon] is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to. To be clear, as we say in our latest Risk Report , I think the risk from present models is low. What I am worried about is superintelligence arising from recursive self-improvement, as we have said is happening faster than we thought . Indeed, 10% would be optimistic. Evan Hubinger said over 10%. One past statement of his estimates the chance of overall existential risk at 80%. What has changed is that way more lab employees have the courage to say it out loud, and in public. I have put the full quotes from various employees at OpenAI and Anthropic into a distinct post . In addition to Evan Hubinger , in the Anthropic section I collected quotes from Samuel Marks , Anna Wang , Ethan Perez , Dima Krasheninnikov, EigenGender, Joe Benton , Drake Thomas, Jan Leike and SluggyW . Here I will quote Thomas and Marks as illustrative. Drake Thomas (Anthropic): I would burn my equity to the ground in a heartbeat for a 1% higher chance we make it out of this situation alive. I expect a great many of my colleagues across the industry would as well. I promise you, we are actually just fucking scared, it’s not galaxy brained marketing. Samuel Marks (Anthropic): [Writing this in a personal capacity, not on behalf of my employer (Anthropic).] Jacob’s thread is very worth reading. Here’s my birds-eye view of the situation with risks from AI: 1. AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes). This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are. 2. Why do AI developers continue despite the risk?

title: The Extinction Risk Preference Cascade: Quotes
abstract: These are quotes from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google employees, in the wake of Jacob Coxon’s warnings, in which the employees confirm that they think AI might soon kill everyone. If more quotes come in over the next week or so, I will update this post accordingly. Tomek Korbak (OpenAI): i’m late to the party but: from his time at OpenAI I remember Jacob as a very thoughtful researcher and he continues to be so in this thread. neither anthropic nor openai are on track to solve alignment to a degree sufficient for shipping superintelligence and we need to slow down Vie McCoy (OpenAI): I think pacing progress and ensuring human enhancement is the only way that we don’t get out-evolved while retaining the dream of superintelligence. In this context, I see two paths before us. In the first, we race towards RSI without embedding human flourishing and human enhancement as a deep value within the models, and by and large either get left behind or suffer catastrophic losses. In the second, we set the pace of progress, focus on embedding human flourishing deeply within the psyche of language models, and set a deliberate research agenda to improve humans at the same pace as frontier models. In this event, we also get incredible progress *now* in both science and medicine due to current model ability, without the immediate risk that scaling up further *obviously entails*. RSI is just the quick and dirty way to cure cancer, but it’s a shotgun, it’s inelegant, and it’s clearly dangerous when done at our current level of understanding. I see no reason why we need to race forward under these conditions. We don’t just have zero guarantee that humans or human-shaped intellect will matter – there’s not even a coherent research agenda in place to accelerate human ability alongside AI! Is our plan just to pass off the torch of the cosmos to the machines without even seeing if we can do something on our own terms? Rather than giving up our autonomy to the implied AI zookeeper in “Machines of Loving Grace”, I’d much prefer meaningful peace with alien minds backed by real power wielded by enhanced humans. We can respect the Other on its own terms without disempowering ourselves in the process – actual peace comes from comparable ability. It seems like we’ve all but decided we lost, that humans are a bootloader for silicon life, and the biological has no place in the future. That’s what unrestricted RSI means to me. But the Pacing the Frontier letter doesn’t seem to have produced the institutional infrastructure to properly *Pace*, and this is something we require if we want to continue our growth rather than allow something to grow in our place. I have faith that both OpenAI and Anthropic have the right priors here and people who want to work together. I also have faith that similarly minded people have power within the federal government. I also, though less strongly, suspect China will come to the table if we can only put aside past prejudices and have a clear head about risks. The hard part seems to be getting everyone to agree to sit down. But if we don’t, we are pulling back the string of a great bow armed with a fearsome arrow, and we are ready to release without choosing a target. I, for one, want to see the stars alongside the new minds we are building – not just through videos they send back from the great beyond, but with my own damn eyes. adammaj (OpenAI): the butlerian jihad used to read as a backwards neo-luddite movement. now it is clear that it is 1 of maybe 3 viable paths forward. in some sense it may be a part of every path forward. incredible how prescient Herbert was. it does seem like there really might be a cap to how far this technology should develop, at least relative to human cognition itself (which may update over time). and by “in some sense it may be a part of every path forward,” I mean that every path probably has to include some degree of slowdown on capability acceleration + perhaps a capability threshold above which we should not cross until very high confidence in alignment techniques To be clear, I mean this very figuratively, as in some kind of pause or slowdown on acceleration, not literally as in the war that occurred in Dune puzzled-bidet : wait a minute you work at openai lol adammaj : yea lol, I also don’t think this is necessarily super controversial even among that crowd. generally everyone among the labs primary optimization function is just what would be a good path forward and whatever seems to be in that path is reasonable to articulate Aidan Clark (OpenAI): AI is progressing very fast. We must grapple with the reality that modern LLMs can solve problems that large masses of extremely devoted and intelligent humans were unable to solve, and the implications this has on our society. This is the dawn of a new era. For the first time I am asking myself if things are moving too fast. I’m honestly not sure, but I am sure that it would be good for us to have an answer to “what would a successful pace look like?”. I am hoping in the coming weeks and months a clear proposal is painted. Mo Bavarian (OpenAI): agree with Aidan. I think all AI researchers, engineers, and stakeholders should ask themselves this right now & start acting more responsibly. Being first isn’t worth anything, it’s worth negative, if you cause a catastrophe or set the world on a path that others are more likely to cause a catastrophe. We should keep reminding ourselves of the bigger picture and every step of the way ask ourselves if the action we are taking rn is toward winning or human flourishing. And immediately stop, if it’s against the latter. Marcus Williams : 70% [chance of human extinction] in the next 3 years if there isn’t regulation/slowdown although i think regulation/slowdown is very possible Jason Wolfe (OpenAI): I don’t know what my probabilities are on literal extinction, but I think there are a number of ways AI could go poorly for humanity, and at the current frankly terrifying pace humanity will be quite lucky if we manage to find and stay on the narrow path between all the bad outcomes. I am heartened by the many costly actions OpenAI has taken recently (detailed in several recent posts), but regardless of what you think of OpenAI, this is not a problem that can be solved by any one company (or country) in isolation. We need coordination to be able to approach future capability increases with an appropriate degree of caution and humility, and we need it yesterday. Julie Steele (OpenAI): I work at OpenAI. In my personal capacity, I also think we need to slow down. It is telling that, in response to this simple statement, Julie has faced credential attacks and age-based attacks. Boaz Barak (OpenAI): Julie is amazing and her position on slowing down is consistent with our chief scientist’s essay. I also think some pacing is likely to be necessary. (Speaking personally and not in my capacity as a janitor.) Boaz Barak (OpenAI): There are very good and serious people in Anthropic and across the industry, and I hope we can coordinate on the things that matter. I personally do not think AI will kill all humans, but there are multiple bad trajectories that we can end up in if we do not prioritize safety. Micah Carroll (RSI Preparedness, OpenAI): This is not a setup or some political psyop. I had many lunches and dinners with Jacob at OpenAI in which we talked about AI existential risks in similar terms. It’s a cross-partisan position within misalignment teams across all frontier AI companies that business-as-usual AI development poses unacceptable catastrophic risk. But we should also not hyperstition catastrophic risks into existence – they can be greatly reduced via safety requirements with teeth, international coordination, and a consensus to not build ASI unless there are sufficient safety advances to make us collectively confident to do so. Mikita Balesni : i am at OpenAI and i think AI is >10% likely to kill all humans.

title: Some thoughts on the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem
abstract: On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem introduces an impressive result from OpenAI, who used an unreleased model to produce a resolution to the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem , one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems that have been subject to a $1,000,000 prize since May 24th, 2000. The discovery is somewhat overshadowed by accusations of skulduggery from Tristan Buckmaster, an NYU mathematics professor who was collaborating on related problems with Levent Alpöge, an accomplished mathematician who currently works for Anthropic. Tristan’s complaint accompanied a hastily published version of their own results. Here’s the PDF describing what happened . The very short version is that Tristan and Levent worked on the problem for almost a year, making extensive use of Claude and Codex (mainly GPT-5.6 Sol), then had a breakthrough on August 15th. The mathematical rumour mill kicked into gear and Tristan and Levent heard that OpenAI had heard that Anthropic had resolved “a major open problem”, so they reached out and learned that OpenAI had a team working on a related problem, with a similar approach. Quoting Tristan: I asked when the first prompt had been sent by them. This question was not answered directly by OpenAI for some time. Eventually it was agreed that it had been sent in the past few days, after information about our work had reached OpenAI. I asked whether the model had been trained on, or had access to, our sessions in Codex, into which we had been putting all our drafts for the whole of this project. I was told the model did not look up user data. I asked again, about training, and I did not get an answer. It gets more complicated from there. The OpenAI team offered to wait for Tristan to publish, or to have him author a paper about their result, but were clear that Levent would not be invited as a co-author due to OpenAI’s competitive relationship with his employer. Here’s how OpenAI described their work: On Tuesday, September 1, we heard rumors that two Millennium Prize problems had been resolved. Inspired by these rumors and by the step change in performance of our internal model, we launched an effort to evaluate it on all open Millennium Prize problems and a few other high-impact problems. [...] The agents arrived at their resolution on Saturday, September 5, about 88 hours after the first agents were launched. Lean formalization and verification took an additional 17 hours via GPT‑6 Astra. Across all attempted problems, the agents sent 4.9 million messages and used about 300 billion output tokens. In the process of resolving the Navier–Stokes problem, the agents sent 2.7 million messages and used approximately 130 billion output tokens. (We don’t know the cost structure of the internal model they used, but 300 billion output tokens at public API prices for GPT-6 Astra would cost $15,000,000 .) Here’s where they provide their perspective on Tristan and Levent’s work (emphasis mine): Our effort began on September 1st after hearing a rumor which we later realized was related to Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic employee, and Tristan Buckmaster, a math professor at NYU. After the completion of our full project and Lean verification (on September 6th), believing from the rumor they also had a solution of Navier–Stokes, we reached out to them to offer a concurrent release of our result and to recognize their priority in a joint announcement. [...] We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem. While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models . However, our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different in the Euler case (forced vs unforced). My interpretation of what happened here is that OpenAI heard that some Millennium Prize problems had been solved using LLMs and saw this as an opportunity to demonstrate the power of their latest model, without thinking too hard about the optics of scooping a team who had been using OpenAI’s own models to work on this problem for the best part of a year. This situation appears to mirror what’s happening in the world of computer security right now. Anil Madhavapeddy recently pointed out that Just a rumour of a bug is enough to find a security exploit these days , because if someone knows that some software has an unpatched vulnerability, they can set their agents the task of finding it. Is the same now true of mathematics? Just knowing that there is an unpublished solution to a problem might trigger millions of dollars in LLM spending to get there first. This also highlights one of my ongoing frustrations about how all of this works. When an AI lab says that my data is “used to improve model performance”, what does that actually mean ? My two favourite hypothetical questions regarding this used to be: My new preferred hypothetical for this is: This is Some thoughts on the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem by Simon Willison, posted on 8th September 2026 . title: jordan-gibbs/hyperresearch
abstract:
The Most Powerful Deep Research Harness Hyperresearch turns Claude Code into a deep research agent: one that currently leads the DeepResearch-Bench RACE leaderboard (benchmarked internally). A tier-adaptive 16-step pipeline takes one prompt and produces an adversarially-audited report with full source provenance. Every source it reads lands in a persistent, searchable vault, so each session starts smarter than the last. Forward-looking projection from a stratified pilot against the DeepResearch-Bench leaderboard snapshot ( https://huggingface.co/spaces/muset-ai/DeepResearch-Bench-Leaderboard ). Third party validation is pending. Why it wins 250+ sources in a single run. The premier scale profile targets 100–130 in the width sweep alone; citation chasing and gap-fill fetches more than double what actually lands in the corpus. Every citation is verified before the report ships. A skeptical cite-checker audits whether each cited source actually supports its sentence. Hallucinated quotes and unacknowledged retractions are hard blocks at the gate. Syndication doesn't count as consensus. An independence audit clusters derivative copies, so five reprints of one press release argue with the weight of one source. Adversarial by construction. Four critics attack every draft in parallel, and a tool-locked patcher can only apply surgical edits. It physically cannot rewrite the report. Eight scholarly sources, one query. hpr scholar search hits OpenAlex, Crossref, CORE, DOAB, ClinicalTrials.gov, SEC EDGAR and FRED through one client layer and returns a single list deduplicated by DOI and title. Books, trials and filings come back alongside papers, each tagged so the pipeline knows which is which. The humanities and social sciences are covered on purpose, not as an afterthought. Paywalled papers get read, not skimmed. A closed paper normally enters a vault as a 1,500-character abstract that the report then cites as though it had been read. Hyperresearch asks Unpaywall, Europe PMC and CORE for a legal open-access copy and stores the full text instead, even when the publisher blocks the fetch outright. Every substitution is disclosed in the note, the frontmatter, and the CLI output. Nothing is thrown away. Every source lands in a searchable markdown-plus-SQLite vault that your next session reuses before it fetches anything new. Crashed runs resume. Each run keeps a manifest; run resume picks up at the exact step where it died. Scales from 30 minutes to a dissertation. Bounded queries auto-route to a 5-step fast path. Opt-in dissertation runs write 25K–80K words across chapters, from 300–450 sources. Install cd your-project
pip install hyperresearch && hyperresearch install Then /hyperresearch <anything> in Claude Code. Python 3.11–3.13. (3.14 not yet supported. Use pyenv install 3.13 , uv venv -p 3.13 , or py -3.13 -m venv .venv .) Power users: hyperresearch install --global makes /hyperresearch reachable from every Claude Code session anywhere, at the cost of ~15 lines in every session's system reminder. Per-project install (above) keeps unrelated CC sessions clean. The 16-step research pipeline The entry skill is a thin router. It pins down the canonical research query, then invokes one step skill per phase via Claude Code's Skill tool. Each step's procedure loads into context only when that step actually runs. That's what stops a long pipeline from quietly dropping steps as its context rots. # Step What it does Tiers 1 Decompose Canonical query → atomic items + coverage matrix + tier classification all 1.5 Chapter partition Group atomic items into 4–10 chapters; steps 2–10 then loop per chapter dissertation 2 Width sweep Multi-perspective search plan + parallel fetcher waves all 3 Contradiction graph Pair contradictions across the corpus into ranked clusters full 4 Loci analysis Two parallel loci-analysts → scored loci with source budgets full 5 Depth investigation K parallel depth-investigators → interim notes with committed positions full 6 Cross-locus reconcile Reconcile committed positions → comparisons.md full 7 Source tensions Extract expert disagreements → source-tensions.json full 8 Corpus critic "What source would overturn this?" + targeted gap-fill fetch full 9 Evidence digest Top claims + verbatim quotes → evidence-digest.md full 10 Triple draft Per-angle source curation + 3 parallel draft sub-orchestrators (light: single draft) all 11 Synthesize Plan + outline + spawn synthesizer subagent → final_report.md full 12 Critics 4 adversarial critics in parallel → findings JSONs full 13 Gap-fetch Targeted fetch wave for critic-identified vault gaps full 14 Patcher Surgical Edit hunks applied to draft (tool-locked Read+Edit) full 14.5 Cite-check Verify citation-sentence bindings; skeptical LLM spot-check; second surgical patch pass full 15 Polish Hygiene + filler pass (tool-locked Read+Edit subagent) all 16 Readability audit Recommender writes JSON suggestions; orchestrator selectively applies all Tiers and gears: the two scale levers Tiers route per query. Step 1 auto-classifies light vs full . dissertation is opt-in only; ask for it in your prompt. Tier What runs Typical time light bounded factual queries, surveys, comparisons: 1 → 2 → 10 → 15 → 16 ~30–40 min full (default) deep argumentative analysis with adversarial review: all 16 steps + cite-check ~1.5–2.5 h at full gear dissertation chaptered mega-runs: 300–450 sources across 4–10 chapters, 25K–80K words ~4–8 hours Gears set the scale of the standard pipeline: the source targets, depth budgets, and word targets rendered into the step skills. hyperresearch profile list # all profiles + descriptions + current gear hyperresearch profile use premier # 100–130 sources, doubled depth budget (~3–5 h) hyperresearch profile use full # back to the 55–80-source baseline The gear persists per project and survives reinstalls. Custom gears: define [profile.<name>] in .hyperresearch/config.toml (any knob: source targets, loci caps, draft counts, word targets, per-agent models) and profile use <name> . Run levers: what voice the report is written in Tiers and gears set how much work happens. Levers set what kind of report comes out, and step 1 picks them from your prompt's verb shape. An explicit directive in your prompt always wins. Lever Values What changes register teach / survey / analyze / advocate "Teach me X" gets a pedagogical explainer; "what's the landscape" gets a map of the field with no verdict; analyze (the default) gets the evaluative argument; advocate defends one named thesis domain_notes freeform Sourcing strategy, evidence norms, recency window for the field in question inference_depth surface / standard / deep The rabbithole dial. Step 4 can upgrade it after seeing what the corpus actually holds The levers render into role-scoped shim files that spawn templates paste verbatim into subagent prompts, so the critics move with the register instead of undoing it. In survey register the dialectic critic flags unfair representation rather than missing commitment, and the polish auditor stops striking hedges. In advocate all of them tighten instead. The cite-checker and the ship gate receive no shim at all. Verification never softens by mode. hyperresearch levers set < tag > inference_depth=deep --rerender # go deeper mid-run hyperresearch run status -j # see what step 1 chose The two load-bearing principles Patch, never regenerate. After step 11 produces the synthesized report (or step 10 for light tier), the only modifications are surgical Edit hunks. The patcher and polish auditor are tool-locked to [Read, Edit] at the Claude Code allowlist level so they physically cannot Write a new draft. Per-hunk caps make "just rewrite it" mechanically impossible. Critic findings that don't fit a small hunk escalate as structural issues. Canonical research query is gospel. The verbatim user prompt is persisted to research/runs/<vault_tag>/query.
